Abbreviated AK; also called a solar keratosis. A precancerous skin growth that occurs on sun-damaged skin. It often looks like a red, tan, or pink scaly patch and feels like sandpaper. Precancerous describes a growth that is not yet malignant; however, if not treated, it is likely to become malignant.

A genetic condition characterized by a deficiency or the absence of pigment in the skin, hair, and irises of the eyes. The result of a missing enzyme that is necessary for the production of melanin. A person with this condition is known as an albino.
Also known as baldness; the partial or complete loss of hair, most commonly on the scalp.

Also known as a lid lift; the surgical reduction of the upper and lower eyelids by removing sagging skin. A small amount of fat from the patient's thighs or buttocks is sometimes injected in the hollow below the eye to improve appearance. Also sometimes performed to improve eyesight limited by drooping eyelids.
A large blister that is usually more than 0.5 cm in diameter (plural, bullae).

Also known as a strawberry birthmark; a soft, raised, pink or red vascular birthmark. A hemangioma is a benign tissue mass made up of newly formed small blood vessels that in birthmarks are visible through the skin.

definition: A cluster of connected furuncles.
An acute, rapidly spreading bacterial infection within the connective tissues that is characterized by malaise, swelling, warmth, and red streaks. Not to be confused with cellulite.
A normal scar resulting from the healing of a wound (plural, cicatrices).

A noninfected lesion formed by the buildup of sebum and keratin in a hair follicle, often associated with acne vulgaris (plural, comedones). A comedo with an obstructed opening is called a whitehead (a closed comedo). A sebum plug that is exposed to air often oxidizes and becomes a blackhead (an open comedo).
The removal of dirt, foreign objects, damaged tissue, and cellular debris from a wound to prevent infection and to promote healing.
An inflammation of the skin. This condition, which takes many forms, is usually characterized by redness, swelling, and itching.
Profuse sweating. A normal condition when brought on by heat or exertion but can also be the body's response to emotional or physical distress.

definition: Atypical moles that can develop into skin cancer.
Commonly known as a bruise; a large, irregular area of purplish discoloration due to bleeding under the skin. The plural form is ecchymoses.
breakdown_text: ecchym: pouring out of juice ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: Also known as atopic dermatitis; a form of persistent or recurring dermatitis usually characterized by redness, itching, and dryness, with possible blistering, cracking, oozing, or bleeding. A chronic condition, most often seen in infants and children, that appears to be the result of a malfunction of the body's immune system.
Redness of the skin due to capillary dilation. Dilation describes the expansion of the capillary.
Abnormal redness of the entire skin surface.
A widespread rash, usually in children. A rash is a breaking out, or eruption, that changes the color or texture of the skin.

A condition in which there is widespread scaling of the skin. Often accompanied by pruritus, erythroderma (redness), and hair loss. May occur in severe cases of many common skin conditions, including eczema, psoriasis, and allergic reactions.

An inflammation of the hair follicles. Especially common on arms, legs, and in the beard area of men. One cause is a bacterium found in poorly chlorinated hot tubs or whirlpools, leading to hot tub folliculitis.
Also known as boils; large, tender, swollen areas caused by a staphylococcal infection around hair follicles or sebaceous glands.

A swelling of clotted blood trapped in the tissues, usually caused by an injury. The body eventually reabsorbs this blood. Often named for the area where it occurs; for example, a subungual hematoma is blood trapped under a finger or toenail.
The presence of excessive body and facial hair in women, usually occurring in a male pattern. Can be hereditary or caused by a hormonal imbalance.
A group of disorders characterized by dry, thickened, and scaly skin. Caused either by the slowing of the skin's natural shedding process or by a rapid increase in the production of the skin's cells.
breakdown_text: ichthy: dry or scaly ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: A highly contagious bacterial skin infection that commonly occurs in children. Characterized by isolated pustules that become crusted and rupture.

An abnormally raised or thickened scar that expands beyond the boundaries of the original incision. A tendency to form keloids is often inherited and is more common among people with dark-pigmented skin.

Any skin growth, such as a wart or a callus, in which there is overgrowth and thickening of the skin (plural, keratoses). Patches of keratosis in the mouth are known as leukoplakia. Note: kerat/o also refers to the cornea of the eye.
breakdown_text: kerat: hard or horny ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: Also known as spoon nail; a malformation of the nails in which the outer surface is concave or scooped out like the bowl of a spoon. Often an indication of iron-deficiency anemia.
breakdown_text: koil: hollow or concave ; onych: fingernail or toenail ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: Also known as painful fat syndrome; a chronic abnormal condition characterized by the accumulation of fat and fluid in the tissues just under the skin of the hips and legs. Usually affects women and even with weight loss this localized excess fat does not go away. Not to be confused with lymphedema.

A benign, slow-growing fatty tumor located between the skin and the muscle layer. Usually harmless, and treatment is rarely necessary unless the tumor is in a bothersome location, is painful, or is growing rapidly.
Also known as a macula; a discolored flat spot that is less than 1 cm in diameter. Freckles, or flat moles, are examples of macules.

Abbreviated MM; also known as melanoma; a type of skin cancer that occurs in the melanocytes. The most serious type of skin cancer, and often the first signs are changes in the size, shape, or color of a mole.

Also known as chloasma or the mask of pregnancy; a pigmentation disorder characterized by brownish spots on the face. Can occur during pregnancy, especially among women with dark hair and fair skin, and usually disappears after delivery.

Abbreviated NF; a rare, severe infection caused by group A strep bacteria, which are also known as flesh-eating bacteria. These bacteria normally live harmlessly on the skin; however, if they enter the body through a skin wound, this serious, sometimes fatal, infection can result.
Commonly known as an ingrown toenail. The edges of a toenail, usually on the big toe, curve inward and cut into the skin. The affected area is prone to inflammation or infection.
breakdown_text: onych/o: fingernail or toenail ; crypt: hidden ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: A fungal infection of the nail. Depending on the type of fungus involved, can cause the nails to turn white, yellow, green, or black and to become thick or brittle.
breakdown_text: onych/o: fingernail or toenail ; myc: fungus ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: A benign, superficial, wart-like growth on the epithelial tissue or elsewhere in the body, such as in the bladder.
A small, raised red lesion that is less than 0.5 cm in diameter and does not contain pus. Small pimples and insect bites are types of papules.
An acute or chronic infection of the skin fold around a nail.
breakdown_text: par-: near ; onych: fingernail or toenail ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: An infestation with lice. In order to get rid of the infestation, the lice eggs, which are known as nits, must be destroyed.
Very small, pinpoint hemorrhages that are less than 2 mm in diameter (singular, petechia). Sometimes result from high fevers.

Also known as a decubitus ulcer or bedsore; an open ulcerated wound that is caused by prolonged pressure on an area of skin over a bony prominence, such as heels, elbows, hips, and spine. Without proper care, these sores quickly become seriously infected and can result in tissue death. Often starts as a deep tissue injury, or damage to the tissues under intact skin.
Also known as itching; associated with most forms of dermatitis. Note that this term ends in -us, not -is.
breakdown_text: prurit: itching ; -us: a singular noun ending

definition: Abbreviated Ps; a common skin disorder characterized by flare-ups in which red papules covered with silvery scales occur on the elbows, knees, scalp, back, or buttocks.
The appearance of multiple purple discolorations on the skin caused by bleeding underneath the skin. These areas are smaller than an ecchymosis and larger than petechiae.
Producing or containing pus.
Also known as a facelift; the surgical removal of excess skin and fat from the face to eliminate wrinkles.

Also known as adult acne; characterized by tiny red pimples and enlarged blood vessels on the face. A chronic condition of unknown cause that usually develops in individuals with fair skin between 30 and 60 years of age.

A skin infection caused by an infestation of itch mites. These tiny mites cause small, itchy bumps and blisters by burrowing into the top layer of human skin to lay their eggs. Medications applied to the skin kill the mites; however, itching may persist for several weeks.
Abbreviated SCD; an autoimmune disorder in which the connective tissues become thickened and hardened, causing the skin to become hard and swollen. Can also affect the joints and internal organs.

An inflammation sometimes resulting from overactivity of the sebaceous glands that causes scaling and itching of the upper layers of the skin or scalp. Extensive dandruff is a form of seborrheic dermatitis, as is the scalp rash in infants known as cradle cap.
breakdown_text: seb/o: sebum ; -rrheic: pertaining to flow or discharge

definition: Abbreviated SCC; originates as a malignant tumor of the scaly squamous cells of the epithelium; however, it can quickly spread to other body systems. These cancers begin as skin lesions that appear to be sores that will not heal or that have a crusted look.

Abbreviated SLE; also known as lupus; an autoimmune disorder characterized by a red, scaly rash on the face and upper trunk. In addition to the skin, this condition also attacks the connective tissue in other body systems, especially in the joints.

A fungal infection that can grow on the skin, hair, or nails; also known as ringworm, not because a worm is involved, but because as the fungus grows on the skin, it spreads out in a worm-like circle. Tinea does not create this pattern when it grows on the nails.
Also known as hives; itchy wheals caused by an allergic reaction.
Also known as warts; small, hard skin lesions caused by the human papillomavirus (singular, verruca). Plantar warts are verrucae that develop on the sole of the foot.

A skin condition resulting from the destruction of the melanocytes due to unknown causes. Causes irregular patches of white skin, a process known as depigmentation. Hair growing in an affected area may also turn white.
Also known as a welt; a small bump that itches. Wheals can appear as urticaria, or hives, as a symptom of an allergic reaction.
Also known as xerosis; excessively dry skin.
The system made up of the skin and its related structures. The term integument comes from the Latin word meaning to cover or enclose.

The protective outer layer covering the external surfaces of the entire body. Waterproofs the body and prevents fluid loss, blocks the entrance of pathogens, is the major receptor for the sense of touch, and helps synthesize vitamin D from the sun's ultraviolet light while screening out some harmful ultraviolet radiation. The average adult has 22 square feet of skin, making it the largest bodily organ.
Glands located in the dermis layer of the skin and closely associated with hair follicles that secrete sebum (oil) that lubricates the skin and discourages the growth of bacteria on the skin.

Also known as sudoriferous glands; tiny, coiled glands found on almost all body surfaces that help regulate body temperature and water content by secreting sweat. A small amount of metabolic waste is also excreted. The two types are apocrine glands, found at hair follicles, and eccrine glands, which open onto the skin and are most numerous in the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and the forehead.
Pertaining to the skin.
The outermost layer of the skin, made up of several specialized epithelial tissues. Does not contain any blood vessels or connective tissue and is therefore dependent on lower layers for nourishment.
breakdown_text: epi-: above or upon ; derm: skin ; -is: a noun ending

definition: Tissues that form a protective covering for all of the internal and external surfaces of the body.
Tissue that forms the upper layer of the epidermis, consisting of flat, scaly cells that are continuously shed. Squamous means scale-like.
The lowest layer of the epidermis, where new cells are produced and then pushed upward. When these cells reach the surface, they die and become filled with keratin.
A fibrous, water-repellent protein. Soft keratin is a primary component of the epidermis; hard keratin is found in the hair and nails.
Special cells found in the basal cell layer that produce and contain a dark brown to black pigment known as melanin.

The pigment that determines the color of the skin, depending upon the type and amount present. Also produces spots of color such as freckles and age spots, and protects the skin against some of the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun.
Abbreviated UV; refers to light that is beyond the visible spectrum at the violet end. Some UV rays help the skin produce vitamin D; other rays damage the skin.

Also known as the corium; the thick layer of living tissue directly below the epidermis. Contains connective tissue, blood and lymph vessels, nerve fibers, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands. Sensory nerve endings here are the sensory receptors for stimuli such as touch, temperature, pain, and pressure.
Means glue; a tough yet flexible fibrous protein material found in the skin and also in the bones, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments.
Cells found in the connective tissue of the dermis that respond to injury, infection, or allergy by producing and releasing substances, including heparin and histamine.
An anticoagulant released in response to an injury. An anticoagulant prevents blood clotting.
A substance released in response to allergens that causes the symptoms of an allergic response, including itching and increased mucus secretion.
The layer located just below the layers of the skin that connects the skin to the surface muscles. Made up of loose connective tissue and adipose tissue.
Fat.

A term used to describe deposits of dimpled fat around the buttocks and thighs. Not a scientific term; medical authorities agree that cellulite is simply ordinary fatty tissue. Do not confuse with cellulitis.
Also known as fat cells; predominant in the subcutaneous layer where they manufacture and store large quantities of fat.

An oily substance released through ducts opening into the hair follicles that moves onto the surface and lubricates the skin. Because sebum is slightly acidic, it discourages the growth of bacteria on the skin.
The openings on the surface of the skin that act as the ducts of the sweat glands.

Commonly known as sweat; secreted by sweat glands and made up of 99% water plus some salt and metabolic waste products. Evaporation cools the body. Normally, up to one quart of liquid is perspired daily.
The production and excretion of perspiration.

Rod-like structures composed of tightly fused, dead protein cells filled with hard keratin. The darkness and color of the hair is determined by the amount and type of melanin produced by the melanocytes that surround the core of the hair shaft.
The sacs that hold the root of the hair fibers. The shape of the follicle determines whether the hair is straight or curly.

Tiny muscle fibers attached to the hair follicles that cause the hair to stand erect. In response to cold or fright, these muscles contract, causing raised areas of skin known as goose bumps, which reduces heat loss through the skin.
Commonly known as a fingernail or toenail (plural, ungues); the keratin plate that protects the dorsal surface of the last bone of each finger and toe.
The translucent part of the nail, closely molded to the surface of the underlying tissues. Made up of hard, keratinized plates of epidermal cells.
The skin underneath the nail plate, which joins the nail body to the underlying connective tissue and nourishes the nail. The blood vessels here give the nail its characteristic pink color.
The portion of the nail not attached to the nail bed that extends beyond the tip of the finger or toe.
A pale half-moon-shaped region at every nail root, generally most easily seen in the thumbnail (plural, lunulae). The active area of the nail, where new keratin cells form.
A narrow band of epidermis attached to the surface of the nail just in front of the root, protecting the new keratin cells as they form.
The part of the nail that fastens the nail to the finger or toe by fitting into a groove in the skin.
A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating disorders of the skin.
A physician who specializes in the surgical restoration and reconstruction of body structures. The term plastic is related to the suffix -plasty, meaning surgical repair.
Plastic surgeons who perform operations such as breast augmentation, liposuction, and facelifts that are usually done for aesthetic rather than medical reasons.

Commonly known as acne; a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by pustular eruptions of the skin caused by an overproduction of sebum around the hair shaft. Although often triggered by hormones in puberty and adolescence, it also occurs in adults. Vulgaris is a Latin term meaning common.
Often referred to as a sebaceous cyst; a closed sac found just under the skin that contains yellow, fatty material and is usually found on the face, neck, or trunk.
A benign skin growth that has a waxy or pasted-on look. Can vary in color from light tan to black and occurs most commonly in adults over the age of 50.
Also known as hypohidrosis; the abnormal condition of lacking sweat in response to heat. People with anhidrosis are at risk for heat stroke.
breakdown_text: an-: without ; hidr: sweat ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: Also known as prickly heat; an intensely itchy rash caused by blockage of the sweat glands by bacteria and dead cells.

Also known as sunstroke; a medical emergency caused by prolonged exposure to high temperatures. Characterized by a core temperature of at least 104° F, altered mental state, and racing heart rate, and can cause organ swelling and death.
A condition of excessive sweating in one area or over the whole body.
breakdown_text: hyper-: excessive ; hidr: sweat ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: Commonly known as night sweats; the occurrence of hyperhidrosis during sleep. Potential causes include menopause, certain medications, and some infectious diseases.
A superficial bacterial infection of the hair shafts in areas with extensive sweat glands, such as the armpits. Axillaris is Latin for axillary (axill means armpit, and -ary means pertaining to).
breakdown_text: trich/o: hair ; myc: fungus ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: An autoimmune disorder that attacks the hair follicles, causing well-defined bald areas on the scalp or elsewhere on the body. Often begins in childhood. Areata means occurring in patches.
Abbreviated AT; an uncommon condition characterized by the loss of all the hair on the scalp.
Abbreviated AU; the total loss of hair on all parts of the body. Universalis means universal.

The most common type of hair loss. Androgenic means referring to androgens, the hormones involved in the development and maintenance of masculine characteristics. In men it is called male pattern baldness; in women it is called female pattern baldness and rarely leads to total hair loss.

The abnormal curving of the nails that is often accompanied by enlargement of the fingertips. Can be hereditary but is usually caused by changes associated with oxygen deficiencies related to coronary or pulmonary diseases such as lung cancer.
Also known as onychitis; an inflammation of the bed of the nail that often results in the loss of the nail.
breakdown_text: onych: fingernail or toenail ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: The separation of the nail plate from the nail bed. Usually painless, and can be caused by a localized allergic reaction, fungal infection, or psoriasis.

A condition where one or more areas of the skin develop dark, velvety areas of discoloration, usually in skin folds. Can be a sign of a disease such as cancer or type 2 diabetes or a reaction to a medication.
Also known as solar lentigines (singular, lentigo) or liver spots; discolorations caused by sun exposure. Although harmless, these spots sometimes resemble skin cancer growths.
An injury to underlying tissues without breaking the skin, characterized by discoloration and pain. The discoloration is caused by an accumulation of blood within the skin.
A pathologic change of the tissues due to disease or injury. Skin lesions are described by their appearance, location, color, and size as measured in centimeters.
Also known as scab; a collection of hard, dried serum and blood that forms as a barrier over a partial-thickness wound.
Dead crust-like tissue found in a full-thickness wound. Usually brown or black, and often a natural stage of wound healing.
The wearing away of a surface, such as the epidermis of the skin or the outer layer of a mucous membrane. Can also describe the progressive loss of dental enamel.
A solid, raised skin lesion that is larger than 0.5 cm in diameter and deeper than a papule. In acne vulgaris, nodules can cause scarring.

A scaly, solid raised area of closely spaced papules. For example, the lesions of psoriasis are plaques. The term also means a fatty buildup in the arteries and a soft substance that forms on the teeth.
Flakes or dry patches made up of excess dead epidermal cells. Some shedding is normal; excessive shedding is associated with skin disorders such as psoriasis.
A closed pocket containing pus that is caused by a bacterial infection. Can appear on the skin or within other structures of the body.
A fluid, such as pus, that leaks out of an infected wound.
An abnormal sac containing gas, fluid, or a semisolid material. Can also refer to a sac or vesicle elsewhere in the body. The most common type of skin cyst is a sebaceous cyst.
Also known as a pimple; a small, circumscribed lesion containing pus. Circumscribed means contained within a limited area. Can be caused by acne vulgaris, impetigo, or other skin infections.
A small blister, less than 0.5 cm in diameter, containing watery fluid. For example, the rash of poison ivy consists of vesicles.
An injury in which superficial layers of skin are scraped or rubbed away.
A groove or crack-like break in the skin, such as the breaks in the skin between the toes caused by tinea pedis, or athlete's foot. Also describes folds in the contours of the brain.
A torn or jagged wound or an accidental cut wound.
An accidental puncture wound caused by a used hypodermic needle, potentially transmitting an infection. A puncture wound is an injury caused by a pointed object piercing the skin.
An open lesion of the skin or mucous membrane resulting in tissue loss around the edges. Ulcers also occur inside the body.
A mole or blemish on the skin present at birth or shortly thereafter. Some birthmarks fade as a child gets older.
Birthmarks that include nevi, also known as moles, as well as café-au-lait spots and other irregularities in skin color.

Also known as a Mongolian spot; a benign blue-grey birthmark commonly found on the back, buttocks, or shoulders of Asian, African-American, Polynesian, and Native American babies. Caused by melanocytes that did not migrate to the surface of the skin before birth, and can resemble a bruise. Usually fades by puberty.
Birthmarks caused by blood vessels close to the skin's surface. The most common type of birthmarks and include macular stains, hemangiomas, and port-wine stains.
Flat, red irregularly shaped birthmarks that are also called salmon patches for their shape, or angel kisses depending on their location.
A flat vascular birthmark made up of dilated blood capillaries, creating a large, reddish-purple discoloration on the face, neck, arms, or legs. Will not resolve without treatment.

Abbreviated CD; a localized rash caused by repeated contact with an irritant, such as harsh cleaning chemicals, or an allergen, such as latex gloves or poison ivy. Can cause localized redness, blisters, swelling, and itching.

Dermatitis caused by the friction of skin rubbing together in skin folds, such as those in the armpits, groin, and under the breasts. The damage makes the skin more susceptible to fungal or bacterial infections.

Also known as fifth disease; a mildly contagious viral infection that is common in childhood. Produces a red, lace-like rash on the child's face that looks as if the child has been slapped. Called fifth disease for its place on a list of six common childhood diseases that can cause an exanthem.

A skin disorder resulting from a generalized allergic reaction to an illness, infection, or medication. Affects the skin, the mucous membranes, or both, and is characterized by a rash that may appear as nodules or papules, macules, or vesicles or bullae.

Also known as chilblains; a purple-red inflammation that occurs when the small blood vessels below the skin are damaged, usually due to exposure to cold and damp weather. When warmth restores full circulation, the affected areas begin to itch; however, they usually heal without treatment.
A form of erythema in which skin cells are damaged by exposure to the ultraviolet rays in sunlight. This damage increases the chances of later developing skin cancer.
A general term used to denote skin lesions or eruptions of any type that are not associated with inflammation.
Also known as bulbous nose; usually occurs in older men. Characterized by hyperplasia (overgrowth) of the tissues of the nose and is associated with advanced rosacea.
A mild viral infection common in children under 5 years of age. Characterized by sores in the mouth and throat and a rash on the hands and feet.
A viral infection that causes small, raised lesions, called mollusca. Mollusca are white, pink, or flesh colored with a dimpled center, and may occur anywhere on the body.

Death of tissue, most commonly caused by a loss of circulation to the affected tissues. The tissue death is followed by bacterial invasion that causes putrefaction, and if this infection enters the bloodstream, it can be fatal. Putrefaction is decay that produces foul-smelling odors.
Any acute, inflammatory, pus-forming bacterial skin infection such as impetigo.
Any abnormal condition or disease caused by a fungus.
breakdown_text: myc: fungus ; -osis: abnormal condition or disease

definition: A fungal infection found on the scalps of children. Capitis means head.
A fungal infection of the skin on the body. Corporis means body.
Also known as jock itch; a fungal infection found in the genital area.
Also known as athlete's foot; a fungal infection most commonly found between the toes. Pedis means feet.
Also known as pityriasis versicolor; a fungal infection that causes painless, discolored areas on the skin. Versicolor means a variety of color.
The dwelling of microscopic parasites on external surface tissue. Some parasites live temporarily on the skin; others lay eggs and reproduce there.
An infestation with head lice.
An infestation with body lice.
An infestation with lice in the pubic hair and pubic region.

A thickening of part of the skin on the hands or feet caused by repeated rubbing. A clavus, or corn, is a callus in the keratin layer of the skin covering the joints of the toes, usually caused by ill-fitting shoes.
The tissue that normally forms during the healing of a wound. Eventually forms the scar.
Also known as a mole; a small, dark skin growth that develops from melanocytes in the skin (plural, nevi). Normally, these growths are benign.
A general term used most commonly to describe a mushroom-like growth from the surface of a mucous membrane, such as a polyp in the nose. Not necessarily malignant.
Also known as acrochordon; small, flesh-colored or light-brown polyps that hang from the body by fine stalks. Benign and usually develop in skin folds of the neck, groin, or armpits.

A malignant growth on the skin which can have many causes, including repeated severe sunburns or long-term exposure to the sun. Affects about one in five Americans in his or her lifetime. The three main types are basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma.

Abbreviated BCC; a malignant tumor of the basal cell layer of the epidermis. The most common and least harmful type of skin cancer because it is slow growing and rarely spreads to other parts of the body. Lesions occur mainly on the face or neck, tend to bleed easily, and are usually pink and smooth and raised with a depression in the center.
A way to remember the signs of melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter larger than a pencil eraser, and Evolving by changing in size, shape, shade, or color.

An injury to body tissues caused by heat, flame, electricity, sun, chemicals, or radiation. Severity is described according to the percentage of the total body skin surface affected (more than 15% is considered serious) and the depth or layers of skin involved.
Also known as a superficial burn; no blisters; superficial damage to the epidermis.
Also known as a partial thickness burn; blisters, damage to the epidermis and dermis.
Also known as a full thickness burn; damage to the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous layers, and possibly also the muscle and bone below.
The removal of a small piece of living tissue for examination to confirm or establish a diagnosis.
breakdown_text: bi: pertaining to life ; -opsy: view of

definition: A biopsy in which a piece, but not all, of the tumor or lesion is removed.
A biopsy in which the entire tumor or lesion and a margin of surrounding tissue are removed. Excision means the complete removal of a lesion or organ.
A biopsy in which a hollow needle is used to remove a core of tissue for examination.

Also referred to as skin scraping; a technique in which cells are scraped from the tissue and examined under a microscope. Exfoliation is the removal of dead epidermal cells, often through sanding or chemabrasion, and is sometimes done for cosmetic purposes.
Abbreviated SPF; a measure of the strength of sunscreen that blocks out the harmful ultraviolet B (UVB) rays. Some sunscreens also give protection against ultraviolet A (UVA) rays.
Also known as dermatoplasty; the replacement of damaged skin with healthy tissue taken from a donor site on the patient's body.
The destruction of tissue by burning.
Also known as a chemical peel; the use of chemicals to remove the outer layers of skin to treat acne scarring, fine wrinkling, and keratoses.
Also called freezing; the destruction or elimination of abnormal tissue cells, such as warts or tumors, through the application of extreme cold by using liquid nitrogen.
The removal of material from the surface by scraping. One use is to remove basal cell tumors.
Abbreviated I&D; a procedure in which pressurized fluid is used to clean out wound debris.

A form of abrasion involving the use of a revolving wire brush or sandpaper. Used to remove acne and chickenpox scars as well as for facial skin rejuvenation. Microdermabrasion removes only a fine layer of skin, so the results are temporary.

A surgical technique performed in conjunction with curettage in which layers of tissue are destroyed using an electric spark and then scraped away. Primarily used to eliminate small superficial growths and to seal off blood vessels; also known as electrodesiccation and curettage (EDC).
A cut made with a surgical instrument.
Abbreviated I&D; an incision (cutting open) of a lesion, such as an abscess, and the draining of the contents. The abbreviation I&D is used for both irrigation & debridement and incision & drainage.

A technique used to treat various types of skin cancer. Individual layers of cancerous tissue are removed and examined under a microscope one at a time until a margin that is clear of all cancerous tissue has been achieved.

An acronym in which the letters stand for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Used to treat skin conditions and other disorders of the body. A laser tube can be filled with a solid, liquid, or gas substance that is stimulated to emit light at a specific wavelength.
The use of natural or artificial light to treat skin conditions such as vitiligo and eczema. One type is photodynamic therapy.

Abbreviated PDT; also known as blue-light therapy; a technique used to treat damaged and precancerous skin, as well as various types of cancer. A photosensitizing drug is administered topically or by injection, followed by an incubation period and exposure to a specific wavelength of light. When activated, the photosensitizers produce a form of oxygen that kills nearby cells.

A topical chemotherapy cream used to treat basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratoses by targeting fast-growing cells. Applied regularly for 2 to 12 weeks, and causes localized irritation, redness, and swelling.
A class of chemical compounds derived from vitamin A that are used in skin care and treatment because of their effect on epithelial cell growth. Can make the skin burn more easily.
Known by its trade name of Accutane; a powerful retinoid taken in pill form for the treatment of severe acne.
The active ingredient in Retin-A and Renova, which are used to treat sun-damaged skin, acne, and wrinkles.

Drugs such as hydrocortisone and other more potent variations used in the treatment of various skin disorders and diseases. Derivatives of the natural corticosteroid hormones produced by the adrenal glands; must be used cautiously to avoid potential side effects, which can include irreversible thinning of the skin.
Not clogging pores; describes over-the-counter face washes containing salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide recommended for treating acne.

A formulation of botulinum toxin, the same neurotoxin responsible for botulism. When injected in small, sterile doses into muscles on the forehead, it can temporarily block the nerve signals to the injected muscle for up to 3 to 4 months, reducing moderate to severe frown lines between the eyebrows. Also used therapeutically to treat migraines, overactive bladder, strabismus, and muscle spasms.

A form of soft-tissue augmentation used to soften facial lines or scars or to make lips appear fuller. Tiny quantities of collagen are injected under a line or scar to boost the skin's natural supply of collagen. The effect usually lasts for 3 to 12 months.
The use of electric current to destroy hair follicles in order to produce the relatively permanent removal of unwanted hair.
The use of lasers to damage hair follicles in order to produce the relatively permanent removal of unwanted hair, such as for patients with hirsutism.
The surgical removal of fat from beneath the skin to improve physical appearance.
Also known as suction-assisted lipectomy; the surgical removal of fat beneath the skin with the aid of suction.

The treatment of spider veins by injecting a saline sclerosing solution into the vein. This solution irritates the tissue, causing the veins to collapse and disappear. Spider veins are small, nonessential veins that can be seen through the skin, often on the legs.
